{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River at night, I bid a guest farewell;  
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.  
The host dismounts, the guest remains aboard his boat;  
We raise our cups to drink, but no music fills the air.  
Though tipsy, joy is absent; we face a bleak parting.  
At the moment of goodbye, vast waters hold the moon’s reflection.  

Suddenly, over the water, come the sounds of a pipa.  
The host forgets to return home; the guest delays departure.  
Following the sound, I softly ask who plays,  
But the pipa pauses; she hesitates to speak.  
We move our boats close together and invite her to join,  
Add more wine, relight the lamps, and reopen the feast.  
Called upon thousands of times, only then does she appear,  
Still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.  

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;  
Before the melody forms, feeling already flows forth.  
Each string restrains emotion; every note carries thought,  
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled ambitions.  
With lowered brows, she plays on without pause,  
Pouring out the endless matter of her heart.  

Light touches, slow rolls, slides and picks—  
First performing *Nishang Yuyi*, then *Liuyao*.  
The great strings thunder like sudden rain;  
The small strings whisper like private talk.  
Thundering and whispering intermingle freely;  
Large and small pearls fall onto a jade plate.  

Sweet as birdsong sliding beneath blossoms,  
Muffled as a spring struggling under ice.  
The icy spring grows cold and sluggish; the strings seem to freeze;  
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.  
A hidden sorrow and silent regret arise anew;  
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.  

Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water spurts forth;  
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and spears ring.  
When the piece ends, she draws the pick across the center;  
All four strings emit one sound like tearing silk.  

East boats and west barges lie in hushed silence;  
Only in the heart of the river does the autumn moon shine white.  
She hesitates, inserts the pick into her strings,  
Adjusts her clothes, rises, and composes her features.  

She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital;  
My home was near Shama Ling.  
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;  
My name adorned the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.  
After finishing a tune, even master players would admire;  
When fully made up, courtesan Qiuniang herself envied me.  

Young men of the Five Tombs vied to offer gifts;  
For one song, bolts of red silk were countless.  
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time;  
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.  
This year laughter followed next year’s joy;  
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed lightly away.  

Then my brother joined the army; my aunt died;  
Days went by, months came; age dulled my beauty.  
At my door, visitors dwindled; carriages grew sparse.  
Getting old, I married a merchant,  
Who values profit above all and neglects partings.  
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
Him gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;  
Surrounding the vessel, bright moonlight lies on cold waters.  

Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;  
Waking, I wept in my sleep, tears staining my makeup red."  

I heard the pipa and sighed;  
Hearing this story, I moaned again.  
We are both wanderers fallen far from home;  
Since we meet, why care if we knew each other before?  

I left the imperial capital last year,  
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.  
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;  
All year long, I hear no strings nor flutes.  
Living near the Pen River, low and damp,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.  
What do I hear at dawn and dusk here?  
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in grief.  
On spring rivers with morning blossoms, on autumn nights with full moons,  
Often I take wine and pour it alone.  

Is there no mountain song or village flute?  
Their harsh, grating tones are painful to the ear.  
Tonight, hearing your pipa words,  
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.  
Please, do not refuse to sit down and play another tune;  
For you, I shall compose the *Song of the Pipa*.  

Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,  
Sat down again, and hurriedly plucked the strings faster.  
The mournful notes differed from those played before;  
The whole audience listened again, covering their faces in tears.  
Who among them shed the most tears?  
The Blue-robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou."}

By the Xunyang River on an autumn night I saw a friend depart,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the cold.
I dismounted; he stood aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings were near.
Drunk, we found no joy—parting grew bitter still,
and when we parted, the vast river drowned the moon.

Then, suddenly, from the water came a pipa's cry—
I forgot my home, my guest forgot to sail.
We followed the sound, asking softly who played,
but the music paused as if she meant to speak, then held her tongue.
We shifted boats to reach her, begged her to appear,
refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and opened the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand pleas, at last she came,
still half-concealing her face behind the pipa's curve.

She turned the pegs, drew across the strings—three, four notes—
and before a melody formed, feeling had already spoken.
Each string a sigh, each note a grief,
as though telling a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers drifting free,
she poured out all the boundless ache within.
Light gatherings, slow twistings, sweeps and pluckings—
first the "Rainbow Robe," then the "Six Strings of Joy."

The great strings thundered, sharp as sudden rain;
the small strings whispered, soft as lovers' talk.
Loud and soft intertwined, a jostling of pearls—
big and small falling on a jade plate, scattering.
Then a warbler's trill, gliding smooth beneath blossoms;
then a choked brook, struggling under ice.
The frozen spring grew sluggish, strings grew still;
stillness sealed them, sound suspended.
A hidden sorrow, a nameless rage was born—
in that silence, more was said than any sound could say.

Then, like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The song ended; her pick swept once across the center strings—
four notes in unison, like silk torn in two.
East boats, west barges: not a word.
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river's heart.

She sat in thought, set the pick between the strings,
straightened her dress, rose, composed her face.
"I was a girl of the capital," she told us,
"my home beneath the Toad Tomb Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name entered the First Troupe of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished a piece, even great masters bowed;
when I made up my face, even the autumn beauties envied.
Young lords of the Five Tombs vied to tie red silk on me;
one song, and bolts of crimson gauze beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs were snapped keeping time,
blood-red skirts stained dark with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed as though they meant nothing.
Then my brother joined the army, my auntie died,
evenings came and went, and beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, the horses sparse—
too old, I married a merchant's wife.
He prized profit, thought little of farewell;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves, and I guard an empty boat at the river's mouth;
moonlight circles the hull, the water runs bitter-cold.
Deep in the night I dream of girlhood days,
wake weeping, tears cutting red lines down my painted face."

I had sighed already at the pipa; hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both souls cast to the world's far edge—
what need for former knowing in this meeting?
I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted to illness in this Xunyang town.
Xunyang lies remote, without its music;
all year long, no silk strings or bamboo pipes are heard.

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the head of Xunyang River, I bid farewell to my guest by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chilly autumn breeze.
The host dismounted while the guest sat on his boat;
We raised our cups, longing for drink, but lacked music’s sweet note.
Drunken joy failed us as sorrow loomed before parting;
When we said goodbye, vast was the river, drowned in moonlight’s haunting.

Suddenly, over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest held back his ship.
Following the music, I asked softly, “Who is playing?”
The pipa fell silent, its player hesitating to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to appear;
More wine was poured, lights turned up, the feast began anew.
Though called upon many times, she emerged only after long delay,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face shyly away.

She twisted the pegs and plucked three or four strings,
Before forming a tune, emotion already sang.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with thought,
As if telling of ambitions thwarted, dreams lost.
Bowed low, she played freely, fingers moving smoothly,
Expressing all the endless sorrows stored within her.

Light strokes, slow twists, sweeps and picks followed:
First *Neon Garments*, then *Six Strings* unfolded.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain pouring down;
The thin strings whispered like private sighs in town.
Thick and thin mixed together in intricate play—
Like pearls large and small falling into jade plate.

Birds chattering smoothly among flowers below;
Water sobbing under ice where currents flow slow.
Cold springs froze stiff, strings seemed to cease;
Frozen tight, blocked up, sound paused without release.
Yet deep hidden grief and dark resentment stirred—
Silence at this moment spoke louder than words heard.

Then suddenly silver vases burst, water spurting high;
Iron cavalry charged, clashing swords crying.
The song ended, pick drawn across center strings;
One final cry like silk tearing, sharp and fierce rings.

East and west boats fell silent, no word spoken aloud;
Only saw autumn moon white on the river’s broad flood.

She pondered, put away her pick, straightened her dress,
Composed herself solemnly, hiding her distress.
“I am originally a girl from the capital,” she said,
“Living near Hama Ridge, where luxury spread.”
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art so fine;
Registered in First Division of Imperial Music Line.
When songs were done, even great masters bowed in awe;
When makeup was set, beauty queens envied her flaw.

Young men from Five Tombs competed to give gifts red;
For one song alone, countless silks they shed.
Gold-plated combs broke beating time in delight;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine late at night.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment;
Moonlit winds enjoyed carelessly, life’s ornament.

But brother joined army, aunt died too soon;
Days and nights wore on, youth faded, bloom gone.
Door became lonely, horse carriages rare;
Aged and married off to merchant’s wife despair.
He values profit more than love, cares little for stay;
Last month he left to buy tea far away.

Since he went, I guard empty boat at river mouth;
Encircled by bright moon, cold waters surround south.
Late at night, I dream of youthful days past;
Wake crying, tears stain rouge running fast.

Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I groaned again heavily.
“We are both outcasts drifting far from home;
Meeting now, why need we have known before?”

Since last year, I left imperial city throne;
Banished to Xunyang, bedridden, sick alone.
Here land is remote, no music can be found;
All year round, silk and bamboo sounds unbound.
My house lies near Pen River, low and wet ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes’ mournful tear.

Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit night—
Often take wine alone, pour it out in sight.
Are there mountain songs and village flute notes true?
Crude, harsh, noisy—hard to listen to you.

Tonight hearing your pipa speech divine,
Like celestial music, ears clear, soul refine.
Do not refuse, sit down, play another tune;
For you, I compose this ballad of the lute’s moan.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence;
Sat down again, strummed faster, growing violence.
Mournful, unlike previous melody’s grace;
Full room listened, faces buried, tears in place.

Who shed most tears among those present here?
The Jiangzhou Sima, blue robe soaked with fear."}

By the Xunyang River, at night I saw off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.
I dismounted from my horse while my guest was still on his boat;
We raised our wine cups, but there were no flutes or strings to play.
Drunk yet not joyful, we grieved at parting;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, came the sound of pipa music;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure.

Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa music stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats closer together and invited her to meet us;
More wine was added, lamps turned up, and the feast began anew.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-shyly covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before a melody formed, emotion had already arisen.
Each string mournful, each note full of sorrow,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled ambition.
With downcast eyes, she played with ease, pouring forth,
Singing all the endless affairs of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Beats*.

The thick strings thundered like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Thunder and whisper mingled in tangled play,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Bottled and flowing, like birdsong sliding beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing, like spring water struggling under ice.
When cold ice congeals the strings’ flow, silence falls,
And this blocked silence halts the sound briefly.
Then arises a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment—
In that moment, silence surpassed sound.

Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water jets forth,
Or iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the tune’s end, she drew the plectrum across the center strings,
All four chords struck once, tearing silk apart.
East and west boats lay silent, speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon at the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said herself: “Originally a girl from the Capital City,
My home lived near Shrimp-Spider Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
Renowned among the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory.
After finishing a tune, skilled musicians would admire me;
Once fully made-up, even beauty rivals grew envious.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk flowed to me.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passing in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
My brother joined the army, my dear aunt died,
Days and nights passed, fading my youth’s bloom.
Few horses and carriages before my door, neglected,
Aged now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit lightly regarding partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
I wake crying, tears staining my rouge-streaked face.”

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
And hearing these words, I lamented again profoundly.
We are both wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital, demoted,
Lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, I hear no string or bamboo sounds.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings with blossoms, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
They croak and chatter, hard to bear listening.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears find clarity anew.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood still for a long time,
Then sat back down, strumming faster, strings urgent.
Her notes were mournful, unlike those heard before;
Everyone present, hearing them again, wiped away tears.
Who shed most tears in the audience?
The Sima (Prefectural Assistant) of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River at night, I bid farewell to a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill of autumn.
The host alighted from his horse while the guest remained on the boat;
We raised our cups, yet lacked music for the drink.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced our parting, sorrowful indeed,
At the time of separation, vast and misty, the river immersed the moon.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa arose from over the water,
So that the host forgot to return and the guest did not depart.

Seeking the source, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, and she hesitated before speaking.
I moved my boat close and invited her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the banquet.
Called upon her a thousand times, ten thousand calls, she only then emerged,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And even before forming a melody, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed sighs, each note carried longing,
As if recounting a life spent without fulfillment.
Chin lowered, casually she continued to play,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.

Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, and picking—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six-Stringed Tune*.
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like intimate gossip.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in mixed notes,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Melodious as orioles gliding beneath blossoms,
Choked and sobbing like springs flowing under ice.
The cold spring seeped slow, the strings seemed frozen still,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.
Yet another hidden sorrow, unspoken resentment arose—
This silence surpassed even the loudest sound.

Then, suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting with water spilling forth,
Or armored cavalry charging with the clash of blades and spears.
As the piece ended, she drew her plectrum across the center,
One strike of the four strings ripped like tearing silk.

East and west boats fell silent, no one spoke,
Only the white autumn moon was seen in the heart of the river.

After a long pause, she placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and stood up with composed dignity.
She said herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home located near Xiama Ling (Toad Hill).
At thirteen years old, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed among the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished a song, even great masters admired me,
When fully made-up, courtesans like Qiuniang grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to offer gifts,
For one song, countless pieces of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year’s laughter repeated into next year’s,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually by.

"My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away,
Days and nights flew by until my beauty faded.
Before my gate, visitors became few, horses sparse,
Growing older, I married a merchant as his wife.
That merchant values profit above all else, lightly regarding partings,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me here guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.
In the depth of night, I dreamed of youthful days,
Waking in tears, my rouge-stained makeup running down my face."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deep,
And hearing these words, I again murmured in grief.
"We are both lost souls wandering the ends of the earth,
Meeting now, why care if we’ve known each other before?"

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year round, I hear no strings or pipes.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Around my house grow yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing in agony.

Often I take wine and pour it alone.

They are harsh and discordant, unbearable to listen to.

It was as if listening to celestial music, my ears suddenly awakened.
Do not refuse; sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa'."

Then sat back down, tightening the strings which played faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before rose up,
The whole room listened again, all covering faces in tears.
Who shed the most tears among the company?

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

maple leaves and reed flowers shivering in the autumn wind.
I dismounted from my horse; my guest still sat aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet no strings or pipes were near.
Drunk, but no joy—grief pressed upon the parting,
and as we parted, the vast river held the moon submerged.
Then, suddenly, across the water, the voice of a pipa—
the host forgot his way home, the guest held back his sail.

I followed the sound, asking softly, who plays?
The pipa fell silent; the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat alongside, invited her to show herself;
more wine was poured, the lamp turned up, the feast resumed.
A thousand calls, ten thousand summons, and at last she came—
still clutching the pipa, half her face veiled behind it.

She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
before a tune took shape, feeling had already lived.
Each string pressed low, each note steeped in longing,
as if telling a whole life of ambitions unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers moved on their own accord,
pouring out the boundless things the heart could not contain.
She gathered, slowed, twisted, swept, then struck—
first the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six-String Wildwillow*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whispered like lovers' private talk.
Thunder and whisper tangled in the playing—
large pearls, small pearls, all tumbling onto a jade plate.
Then a warbling oriole, gliding beneath blossoms;
then a choked spring, struggling under ice.
The cold water froze, the strings stilled, the sound died away—
died, could not pass, and fell into a pause.
Then rose a secret sorrow, a hidden rage—
and this silence surpassed all sound.

iron cavalry charged, blades and spears clanged.
The song ended—she swept the plectrum across the strings;
four strings struck once, like silk tearing clean.

when I dressed, even Qiuniang envied my face.
The young lords of Five Mausoleums vied to gift me silk—
one song, and bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs shattered against the beat;
blood-red skirts stained where wine cups overturned.
This year laughing, next year laughing again—
autumn moons and spring breezes spent as if they meant nothing.

and evening into morning, my beauty faded.
Before my gate the stirrups grew sparse;
grown old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit and weighs parting lightly—
last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He went, and I kept the empty boat at the river mouth;
moonlight wound around the hull, the water ran cold.

We are both castaways at the edge of the same wide sky—
to meet, why must we have known each other?

banished and bedridden in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here—
all year long, not one string, not one bamboo pipe.
I live near the Pen River, where the ground is low and wet;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo claw around my house.
What do I hear at dawn, at dusk?
Cuckoos crying till blood, gibbons wailing.
On spring river nights, on flower-dawn mornings, on autumn moon evenings,
I drink alone, pouring cup after cup.
Are there no hill songs, no village flutes?
They croak and rattle—too harsh for the ear.

Now the sound was bleak, nothing like before—

By the River Xun, at night, I bid a friend farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the cold autumn chill.
I dismount from my horse, you are already upon the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music to support the toast.
Drunk, yet joyless, as we part in sorrow’s grip,
At the moment of goodbye, the moon sinks deep within the river’s dip.
Suddenly, over the water, the sound of a pipa floats near;
I forget to return, and you delay your departure here.
I follow the sound, asking softly who could be playing so well,
The strings fall silent, and she hesitates before she breaks her spell.
We move our boats closer together and invite her to appear,
Add more wine, relight the lamps, and start the feast anew this year.
Called many times, she finally comes out from behind the screen,
Still holding her pipa close, half-hiding her face unseen.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings, just two or three notes first,
Before the melody begins, her feelings have already burst.
Each string conveys restraint, each note carries a heavy thought,
As if recounting the frustration of a life poorly caught.
Brows lowered, fingers moving with natural ease,
She pours out the endless burdens hidden within her heart’s decrees.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, smearing then picking clear,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings" fill all our ears.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain falling fast,
The thin strings whisper like secrets that cannot last.
Roaring and whispering intermingle in complex play,
Like large pearls and small beads dropping on a jade tray.
Now smooth as birdsong under blossoms, bright and sweet,
Now choked and difficult, like springs flowing beneath ice and heat.
The icy spring chills and stops, the strings seem frozen still,
When they cease to transmit sound, silence holds its will.
A different kind of hidden sorrow and secret hate arises then,
In this absence of sound, feeling speaks louder than noise again.
Then suddenly, as if a silver bottle bursts with water spray,
Or iron cavalry charges forth with swords and lances’ display.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center strings,
All four sound once together, tearing silk with sharp things.
East and west ships lie quiet, voices stilled and mute,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s root.
After pondering long, she puts down the pick among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, collecting dignity it brings.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the Imperial City’s heart,
My home lived by Shama Ling, where arts played a vital part.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, skill complete and true,
Registered in the First Section of the Court Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, great masters were forced to admire,
When I put on makeup, even beauty queens felt fired.
Young men of Five Mausoleums competed to give me gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk covered their lifts.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke beating time’s beat,
Blood-red silk dresses stained by overturned wine, incomplete.
Year after year passed with laughter and mirth,
Autumn moons and spring breezes wasted away, worth untold birth.
But my brother went off to war, and my aunt died too,
Days pass, nights come, and my youthful looks faded from view.
My door became cold and lonely, horses rare to see,
Growing older, I married a merchant, bound to trade and fee.
He values profit high, leaving love aside lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, far and distant.
Gone and returned, I guard this empty boat at the river’s mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, while the river waters grow drouth.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of my young days’ affairs,
I wake crying, tear-stained rouge runs down my cheeks’ despair.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed deeply before,
Hearing these words now, I sigh heavily once more.
We are both people fallen from grace, wandering far from home,
What matters if we met before? We share this loneliness alone!
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital’s grand sight,
Banished and sick, lying low in Xunyang’s dreary plight.
Xunyang is remote, musical sounds are hard to find,
Throughout the whole year, zither and flute notes leave nothing behind.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my house, upset.
What do I hear between dawn and dusk in this place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and apes’ mournful embrace.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take my wine and pour it out, drinking alights.
Is there really no village song or rustic pipe’s tune?
Their harsh, chaotic noises make listening painful soon.
Tonight hearing your pipa speak, like celestial music pure,
My ears become clear for a moment, finding cure sure.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song,
I will compose for you 'The Ballad of the Pipa', strong.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time apart,
Then sat back down, tightening strings, starting fresh start.
Her melody grew desolate, unlike sounds before,
Everyone in the room heard again, weeping at the core.
Who shed the most tears in this gathering sad?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue-green robe wet, made bad."}

I dismounted; my guest was already aboard.
We raised our cups to drink, yet had no strings, no pipes.
Drunk, joyless, the bitter parting drew near—
as we said farewell, the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, pipa strings rang out;
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to sail.
Following the sound I called softly, "Who plays there?"
The pipa paused; she wished to speak but lingered.
We drew our boats together, urged her to appear,
refilled the wine, brought back the lamps, reopened the feast.
A thousand calls, ten thousand urgings—only then she came,
still cradling the pipa, half-veiling her face.
She turned the pegs, let fall two, three stray notes—
before the tune had shape, feeling had already spoken.
Each string suppressed, each note heavy with thought,
as if telling of a lifetime's thwarted will.
Brow lowered, fingers free, note after note,
she poured out all the boundless things in her heart.
Light presses, slow twists, sweeps and plucks again—
first *Rainbow Skirt*, then *Six-String* dance.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whisper like a private murmur.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle and play—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.

then, like a stream choking beneath ice, faint and hard.

at this moment, silence surpasses all sound.

one sweep, four strings, a single cry like tearing silk.

one song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting.

blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.

autumn moons, spring breezes, passed without a thought.
My brother joined the army; my auntie died;
evenings came, mornings went, and my beauty faded.
The door grew cold; horses and riders thinned;
past my prime, I took a merchant for my husband.
He weighs profit against parting and chooses profit;
last month he went to Fuliang to trade in tea.
He left; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth;
moonlight circles the hull; the water is bitter cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of youthful days—
wept in my sleep; my paint-streaked tears ran red."
I heard the pipa and already sighed;
heard these words and sighed again, deeper still.
We are both exiles at the world's far edge—
what need to have known each other before?
"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
demoted, bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, with no music at all;
all year I hear not a thread of silk or bamboo.
My house near the Pen River sits low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring the walls.
From dawn to dusk, what do I hear there?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling grief.
Spring river, flower-mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
I take my wine and pour it down alone.
Aren't there mountain songs and village flutes?

as if celestial music; my ears are cleansed.
Do not refuse to sit and play once more—
I will compose for you this *Song of the Pipa*."
Touched by my words, she stood long in thought,
then sat again, pressed the strings—now faster, fiercer.
Grief upon grief, nothing like the earlier sound;
the whole room, hearing it again, buried their faces and wept.
Who wept the most among them all?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was soaked."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

By the banks of Xunyang River, seeing off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted to greet my guest aboard his boat;
We raised our cups for drink, but lacked music’s charm.
Though drunk, joy was absent as parting drew near;
The vast river reflected moonlight, melancholy and clear.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of pipa strings;
Forgetting my return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the notes, I asked softly who played thus;
The pipa paused, hesitating before speaking up.
I moved my boat closer to invite her forth;
More wine was poured, lamps trimmed, the feast resumed.
After many calls and cries, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned pegs and plucked a few preliminary strings,
Before the tune began, emotion already flowed.
Each string was suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if recounting a lifetime of thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed low, she played on without pause,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, she strummed and picked,
First “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six One” followed next.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate confessions.
Thick and thin mingled in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Birdsong gliding beneath blossoms, smooth and sweet;
Spring streams choked under ice, muffled and hard.
The cold spring froze, the strings stiffened and ceased;
In silence stopped, no sound remained for a while.
Then arose hidden sorrow, dark resentment born—
At that moment, silence surpassed even sound.
A silver vase burst suddenly, water spraying forth;
Iron cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing loud.
Ending the song, she swept the plectrum across the center;
Four strings sounded once, like tearing silk cloth.
East and west boats fell silent, not a word spoken;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river’s heart.
Pensively, she placed the plectrum among the strings;
Adjusting clothes, standing upright, composing her demeanor.
She said: “Originally a girl from the capital city,
My home lay beneath Shama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art;
Fame secured me a place in the first troupe of the Ministry of Music.
After finishing a piece, masters themselves would marvel;
When made up, even beautiful courtesans grew envious.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to tip handsomely;
One performance earned countless bolts of red silk gauze.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs snapped keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.
This year laughter and joy, next year again;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Brother enlisted, aunt died; youth faded day by day;
Her looks aged as morning changed to evening light.
Her doorway became desolate, horses rare;
Growing old, she married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants prize profit, care little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guarded our empty boat at the river mouth;
Moonlight circled the boat, river waters cold.
Late at night, I dreamed of youthful days past;
Waking weeping, tears smeared makeup down my cheeks.”
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already;
Hearing these words, my grief doubled anew.
Both are wanderers fallen afar from home;
Meeting thus, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year, leaving the imperial capital behind,
Banished here, ill and bedridden in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of true music;
All year long, no sounds of silk or bamboo heard.
Living near Pen River, where land lies low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear dawn to dusk in this place?
Cuckoo’s blood-crying, gibbons’ mournful wails.
On spring nights with flowers, on autumn full-moon evenings,
Often I take wine alone, pouring myself drunk.
Are there no folk songs or village flutes?
Rough, cacophonous noises, unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s speech,
It’s like celestial music, clearing my ears anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more;
For you, I shall compose “The Ballad of the Pipa.”
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then returned to seat, tightened strings, tempo sped.
Sorrowful tones unlike those played just now;
Full hall, hearing again, all buried faces in tears.
Who shed most tears among those seated here?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe grew wet."}

大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。

间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the River Xun at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount—my guest is already aboard;
We raise our cups, yet no music fills the air.
Tipsy, joyless, we mourn the parting—
The vast river holds the moon in its depths.
Then, sudden from the water, a pipa's cry!
I forget to go home; my guest forgets to sail.

Following the sound, I ask in the dark: who plays?
The strings fall silent, as if she hesitates to speak.
We draw our boats close and invite her forth;
More wine is poured, the lamps turned up, the feast renewed.
Called a thousand times, she finally comes—
Still cradling the pipa, half veiling her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings—
Before a tune takes shape, feeling already pours forth.
Each string muffled, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
Brows lowered, fingers move at will,
Unraveling all the boundless ache within.
Light press, slow twist, sweep, then pluck—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six-String dance.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Roaring, whispering, tangled together—
Pearls large and small scattering on a jade plate.
Then like orioles singing beneath blossoms, smooth as silk,
Then like a spring choking under ice, slow and hard.
Ice-cold, the strings seize and break;
Seized and broken, sound stills for a breath.
A hidden grief, a buried hate rises—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle bursts—water surges!
Cavalry charges—swords and spears clash!
The tune ends; she strikes the center with her plectrum;
Four strings sound once—like silk tearing.
East boats, west barges: all fall mute.
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her dress, composes her face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home near Toad Mound in the old days.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
Her name was ranked in the First Section of the Academy.
Her playing made the greatest masters bow;
Her beauty drew the envy of every courtesan.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to shower her with silk—
For one song, bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Her jeweled combs shattered keeping time,
Her blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter year after year,
Spring moons and autumn breezes passed carelessly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died—
Dawn to dusk, her beauty faded.
Her door grew cold; horse and saddle rare;
Aging, she wed a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes silver, not her company—
Last month to Fuliang he went to buy tea.
Gone, she keeps watch by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Moonlight wraps the hull; the water bites with cold.
Deep at night she dreams of girlhood—
Weeping, her tears stream through rouge across her face.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
Heard her words and sighed again.
We are both souls adrift, cast to the ends of the earth—
Meeting now, what need of knowing before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, lodging in Xunyang's walls.
Xunyang is remote; no music here—
All year I hear no strings, no pipes.
Near the Pen River, the ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What is heard at dawn, at dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding out their cries; gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
I often take my cup and pour alone.
Are there hill songs and village flutes? Yes—
But harsh and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech;
It is music of immortals—my ears are cleansed anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat, tightened the strings, and played—faster now.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole assembly, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his sleeves soaked through."}

By Bai Juyi  

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismount from my horse while he waits in his boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, yet lack music for the feast.
Drunk but not joyful, we sorrow as parting nears;
At the hour of goodbye, the moon sinks into the vast river’s depths.
Suddenly, over the water, a pipa’s melody is heard:
I forget to return home, and my guest delays his departure.

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays;
The pipa stops, but she hesitates, slow to speak her name.
I move my boat close by, inviting her to show herself;
More wine is poured, lamps are brought back, and the banquet resumes.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;
Before the tune takes form, emotion already breathes.
Each note suppressed, each sound laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, she plays casually, continuing on,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, rubbing then picking—
First she plays the “Rainbow Feather,” then the “Six-String Melody.”
The thick strings rumble like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering, mixed together in play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.

Smooth and flowing, like an oriole singing beneath blossoms;
Choked and sobbing, like a spring struggling under ice.
Ice-cold and stiff, the strings freeze to silence;
Blocked and still, the sound momentarily ceases.

A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise;
This moment of silence surpasses any sound.
Suddenly, as if a silver vase breaks and water bursts forth,
Or iron cavalry charges out with swords clashing and spears ringing.

When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center of the strings;
One final stroke sounds like tearing silk.
Eastward ships and westward boats fall silent;

By the Xunyang River, on a night of seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's breath.
The host dismounts, the guest is on the boat;
they raise their cups, but no strings are here.
Drunk yet joyless, they grieve at parting—
at parting, the vast river holds the moon submerged.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice—
the host forgets his way home, the guest delays his sail.

The pipa stops; the player hesitates to speak.
Boats drawn close, she is invited to appear;
wine is added, lamps turned up, the feast begins anew.
A thousand calls, ten thousand pleads—she finally comes,
still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings;
before a tune is formed, feeling is already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
as if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers move without a plan,
playing out the boundless matters of the heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings*.

The thick strings boom like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whisper like a private murmur.
Booming and whispering interweave—
large pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole's song beneath the blossoms,
choked as a spring trapped under ice.
The icy spring, cold and stalled, the strings grow still;
still and blocked, the sound falls silent for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief, is born—
at this moment, silence surpasses sound.

A silver vase bursts, water gushes out;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends; the pick sweeps across the strings;
one stroke, four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west boats, all fall quiet—
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the pick between the strings,
straightens her dress, rises with a composed face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
my home below the Toad Hill in the city.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name entered the First Section of the Teaching Quarter.
When I finished a piece, even the master players bowed;
when I made my face up, even the beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to bind my hair,
one song earned me bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped at the beat,
blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year, laughter; next year, laughter still—
autumn moons, spring breezes, spent without care.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed on;
evenings came, mornings went, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, the horses and riders few;
growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gain, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard my empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood days;
in the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both drifters at the edge of the world—
what need to have been acquainted before we met?

I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted, bedridden in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music here;
all year long I hear not a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, where the ground is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.

often I pour wine and drink alone.

They are hoarse and harsh, unbearable to the ear.

Tonight I heard your pipa's words—
as if hearing celestial music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece;
for you I shall remake this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
then sat back, drew the strings—the sound grew urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the voice before—
the full room, hearing again, all hid their faces and wept.
Who among them wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked."}

By the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell one night,
Amidst maple leaves and rushes, autumn’s chill was biting tight.
I dismounted while he boarded his boat; we raised our cups to drink,
But found no pipes or strings there—our merriment seemed to sink.
So drunk yet joyless, sorrow loomed as parting drew near,
And when we said goodbye, the moon hung in the misty river clear.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa music drifted through,
Making me forget my way home, stopping my guest’s departure too.
We followed the sound, asking softly who might play,
When the music ceased, a hint of hesitation made us stay.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to come and meet,
Added more wine, relit lamps, and prepared for another treat.
After countless calls she finally emerged, shy and slow,
With her pipa half-obscuring her face, looking down below.
She tuned her strings, plucked three or four notes before the tune began,
Yet emotion flowed already, revealing feelings deep within.
Each string whispered restraint, each note conveyed longing so profound,
As if narrating all the disappointments of her life unbound.
Head bowed low, fingers moving freely, playing on and on,
Telling stories of endless sorrows hidden since dawn to dusk gone.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking with grace,
First “Rainbow Garment,” then “Six Strings,” filling the empty space.
The thick strings thundered loudly like a sudden rainstorm’s roar,
While thin strings chimed gently, like whispers behind a closed door.
Loud and soft intertwined, complex melodies played out,
Like pearls big and small falling into a jade dish, bright and devout.
Chirping like birds sliding smoothly beneath blooming flowers’ shade,
Choking like spring water struggling through ice in cold decay.
The icy spring grew sluggish, strings froze, sound came to halt,
Silence held its breath, deeper than words could ever vault.
A new kind of melancholy stirred, unseen resentment born,
At this moment, silence spoke louder than any sound adorned.
Then suddenly, silver vases burst open with splashing spray,
Iron cavalry charged fiercely, clashing swords ringing far away.
When the song ended, she swept her plectrum across the center stage,
Four strings snapped once, tearing silk with a sudden, sharp rage.
Boats east and west fell silent, entranced by what they heard,
Only seeing autumn moonlight reflecting on the river blurred.
Lost in thought, she placed her plectrum back among the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, composed herself, hiding old distressing things.
She told how she had been a girl from the capital city’s heart,
Living near Shama Ling’s slope, where fame and fortune started.
Thirteen years old, master of pipa, first rank in court’s troupe named,
Her songs made skilled masters marvel, beauty rivalled women famed.
Youths from Five Mounds fought to give her gifts of red silk spun,
One song earned bolts beyond counting, before the day was done.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time, blood-red skirts stained with wine,
Year after year laughter echoed, seasons passed without design.
Brothers marched off to war, aunties died with age’s cruel sting,
Beauty faded morning after evening, losing everything.
Front gate grew lonely, horses rare, she married a merchant bold,
Who valued profit over love, leaving her alone and cold.
Last month he went to Fuliang town to buy tea for sale,
Left her guarding an empty boat by the river’s pale trail.
Moonlight circled the vessel, waters chilled in the night’s depth,
Dreaming of youthful days, tears staining cheeks with wet.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply, grief mixed with regret,
Listening to her story, murmurs arose, emotions set.
We are both wanderers fallen under heaven’s wide dome,
Meeting here, why care if we knew each other at home?
Since last year, I left the imperial city, exiled sick and sore,
To live in Xunyang’s remote land, cut off from arts galore.
No music reached my ears throughout the year, not pipe nor zither sound,
Near Penjiang River, damp and low, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo bound.
What did I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing loud,
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—solitude’s heavy shroud.
Often took wine alone, pouring drinks to ease the pain,
Though mountain songs and village flutes existed all around,
Their crude noises harsh and jarring, unbearable to ground.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s voice, like celestial music sweet,
My ears awakened briefly, finding harmony complete.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece for me,
I’ll compose the “Song of the Pipa” for you, wild and free.
Moved by my words, she stood long, then seated down once more,
Plucking faster, strings growing urgent, opening a new door.
Sorrowful tones unlike before filled every seat with dread,
All present listened anew, covering faces, tears shed.
Who cried most among those gathered? The Jiangzhou Prefect’s blue robe wet."}
